quiz: Look for a structure that stays focused on the role and ends by steering toward a story you want to tell.
Aim for roughly 225 words at a normal speaking pace of about 150 words per minute.
Ask what labelling a teammate with insults tells the interviewer about how you treat people.
Think about the moment right after someone says something that annoys you. What do most people fail to do before they answer?
Consider the timing: when you voice concerns versus how you act once the decision is made.
Escalating over your manager is a big step. Ask which situation is serious enough, and what you should do with your manager first.
A humble-brag sounds like a weakness but is really a compliment. Check each option for a real, specific mistake.
Most of a failure story should cover recovery, root cause and prevention, not the mistake itself.
Ask which lesson someone could check later to see if it was really applied, rather than a general promise.
Saying you are coachable proves nothing. Look for the option made of actions the interviewer could verify.
Good help should leave the teammate more able to do the work alone. Which option grows their skill?
Ask what the interviewer is trying to score when they hear the word we in place of I.
Ask what makes a number believable in an interview, and what happens if you are asked how you measured it.
Think about what happens to a memorised script when the interviewer interrupts you with a follow-up.
Think about how the last line of your intro can shape which question the interviewer asks next.
interview: Describe present, past, future in about 90 seconds, with one scale number, one result, why this company, and a closing hook.
Cover emotional maturity: pausing, talking privately, listening, describing the other person fairly, finding a shared goal and a measurable result.
Walk through steps: manage your own emotion, talk privately, listen and repeat back, name the shared goal, compare options with data, agree next steps.
Define voicing concerns early then fully supporting the decision, and name exceptions like ethics, safety or legal issues.
Cover raising concerns privately, early and with evidence, framing as risk or question, respecting their context, then committing if overruled.
Choose a real, recoverable mistake you caused; spend most time on containment, communication, root cause and prevention; avoid humble-brags and blame.
Describe listening without defending, asking for an example, taking time to reflect, making small changes and checking back later.
Mention private and timely delivery, situation-behaviour-impact, focusing on behaviour, asking their view, and offering concrete help.
Cover noticing signals, asking privately, finding the real gap, right-sized help like pairing, then checking in and stepping back.
List common pitfalls like we instead of I, no numbers, blame, fake weaknesses, rambling, scripts, and suggest a story bank as a fix.
Explain using AI as a tough mock interviewer, not a ghostwriter, practising from bullet skeletons and keeping real details.
Separate team delivery from your personal actions, give specific things you did or decided, credit teammates honestly.
Describe a story bank mapped to themes, identifying the skill being tested, picking the strongest evidence and angling to company values.
